paragraphs.text: This is an informal note by Chris Olah arguing that "distributed representations" — a classic idea where information is spread across many units rather than one unit per concept — actually bundles together two distinct strategies: composition and superposition. The piece works through neuron examples borrowed from Thorpe (1989) to pull these apart and show they behave very differently.

The distinction matters because the two strategies have opposite properties for generalization and for what you can read out with a simple linear function, and because telling them apart is needed to escape the curse of dimensionality and actually understand what a network's units mean.

Composition represents independent features (say, color and shape separately) so n features can combine into exp(n) possible objects, generalizes well, and stays easy to interpret linearly. Superposition instead crams more features into fewer neurons than there are dimensions, letting m neurons encode exp(m) items — but retrieving them requires a non-linearity, and you lose the ability to cleanly read out arbitrary features or combinations with a linear probe.

The two strategies compete for the same representational "volume," so a network can't maximize both at once. But because real features are often sparse — rarely co-occurring — networks can mix the two: composing some features while packing others into superposition in the resulting gaps, as shown in Thorpe's "semi-distributed" example.

fuller.text: This is an informal note by Chris Olah asking what "distributed representations" actually means when a network's features are spread across neurons rather than each neuron standing for one thing. It argues that this label actually hides two distinct strategies: composition and superposition. The piece works through Thorpe's classic neuroscience examples of coding colored shapes to tease the two apart.

The distinction matters because the two strategies have very different properties for generalization and for what can be read out with a simple linear function, yet they are often lumped together and even said to give both benefits at once. Separating them matters most for interpretability: composition lets you understand a network in terms of a small number of independent features, while superposition does not support that kind of readout at all. The note frames this as central to reverse-engineering networks, since escaping the exponential blow-up in possible representations requires decomposing them properly.

Composition means independent features, like color and shape, are represented by separate neurons and combined: this needs fewer neurons than a one-neuron-per-combination "local code," supports generalization across combinations, and stays interpretable even though it can express exponentially many combinations. Superposition instead packs unrelated, non-composing features into the same small set of neurons, so a "dense" code with just 4 neurons can represent 16 distinct combinations, far more than the neuron count, but at the cost of losing linear readout and losing the ability to represent things "in between" categories.

The note argues these two strategies are fundamentally competing ways to use a fixed budget of representational volume: full composition of n features needs exponential space, while superposition can store exponentially many items in that same space only by giving up composition and requiring a non-linearity to retrieve them. They can be mixed when features are sparse, so that composing features leave "holes" that other features can occupy in superposition, as shown by Thorpe's "semi-distributed" example. The conclusion is that these two notions of distributed representation are genuinely in tension, and keeping them distinct is essential for understanding what a network's representations really are.
